<a name="20260911012308"></a>

## Reserving a namespace instead of blanking three suites

*2026-09-11 01:23:08*

[#231](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/231) asked how a test suite is supposed to write codes without those codes
being read as citations. Three suites had answered it with `unlinted-file:`,
which blanks the whole file — 1,038 lines between them, to excuse a couple of
dozen specimen codes. The user's answer in the issue thread was better than
mine: stop trying to make the *codes* invisible and give the fixtures a
*scheme* nobody else can declare.

**What I measured before changing anything.** Deleting the three directives
and running the lint produced exactly three new findings, not the flood I
expected: `ADR-007` (Superseded, 14 sites), `ADR-tmpabcde`, and `DP-018`.
That number is the trap. The other fixture codes in those files —
`DP-4`, `DP-004`, `DP-1`, and the composed `LU-DP-004` — were **silent
because they resolved**. A specimen that resolves is counted as a citation of
a real document and looks exactly like one, forever, until the document it
borrowed moves. The loud findings were the safe ones.

`tests/test_alias_inference.py` turned out to need no directive at all: its
`LIT-…` spellings match nothing here, because this project has no `LIT`
scheme. Invisible by luck, which is the property the whole exercise exists to
stop depending on.

**Why a namespace and not a name.** [#231](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/231)'s comment proposed one reserved
prefix, `FXL`. `tests/test_migrations.py` renames a scheme, so it needs an old
prefix and a new one in the same fixture — with one reserved name the second
falls back to `GP`, which is safe here only because nobody has declared it.
Reserving everything that starts with `FX` costs nothing (the match is on the
leading prefix, so `AFX` is untouched) and makes the second prefix safe by
construction.

**Where the guard could not go.** The obvious place for "refuse this prefix"
is config load. That is self-defeating: fixture projects declare `FXL` on
purpose, so a load-time refusal breaks the mechanism it is protecting. The
check had to run where a human reads it — `lint.run()` — and it is only
harmless there because the suites call individual `check_*` functions rather
than the whole run. That is worth knowing before anyone adds a check the
other way around.

**Fired once on the real case**, as this file's own rule requires. Adding
`[luria.schemes.FXL]` to this project's `luria.toml` and running
`python -m luria.cli lint` produced the violation — and, in the same run, made
**ten fixture codes across 96 citation sites** start reporting as dangling.
That second half is the better evidence: it is the hazard, demonstrated, not
argued.

**Backticks do not mask a reference-status citation, and that is on
purpose.** Writing the ADR, I quoted the specimen codes as evidence —
`` `ADR-007` ``, `` `ADR-tmpabcde` ``, `` `DP-018` `` — assuming inline code
made them mentions. `luria link --fix` agreed and left them alone;
`ref_status.scan()` counted all four sites anyway. Its docstring says so
("deliberately unmasked, unlike the link lint"), and eleven other decisions
already carry `inactive-ok-file: ADR-007` for the same reason. The shorthand
in CLAUDE.md — "codes in backticks are mentions, not citations" — is true of
the *fixer* and not of the *report*, which is the stricter of the two on
purpose: a retired code quoted in prose is still a reader following it
somewhere retired.

**A trap that cost me twenty minutes.** `luria` on `PATH` is a non-editable
install in `dist-packages`, so `luria lint` was running the released 0.15.0
and reporting the new check as absent. It reads the working tree's *record*,
so every measurement of the directive removal above was still valid — but any
measurement of new *code* has to go through `python -m luria.cli`.

<a name="20260911054100"></a>

## Lint only column-0 HTML comments in YAML frontmatter

*2026-09-11 05:41:00*

[#164](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/164) is the Pages-build miss:
PyYAML treats a frontmatter line that *opens* with `<!--` as a mapping key
and keeps the last of two identical keys, while Quartz rejects both. The
first cut of the lint check stripped leading whitespace before looking for
`<!--`, which would also flag an indented comment inside a folded scalar
such as `summary: >-`.

That spelling is legal YAML content. Column 0 is what makes PyYAML invent a
key; an indented `<!--` is just text. No live vault entry used that shape
when the check landed, but the first one that does is likely to be the
entry that explains this bug.

The check now uses `line.startswith("<!--")`. A `#` comment still stays
silent. Duplicate unindented keys are unchanged.

<a name="20260911235842"></a>

## A typed-lineage graph on every page that has lineage

*2026-09-11 23:58:42 · site · record*

**The ask was to replace Quartz's graph with strata-g's; the measurement said
don't, so this adds one instead.** The request was straightforward — luria's
sites already render Quartz's `Component.Graph`, strata-g exports a
self-contained interactive graph viewer, swap one for the other. Before
building it, count what the replacement would draw. On this record: **61 typed
edges across 110 scheme documents**, so 52 of them (47%) have any typed edge at
all, with degrees 1–6 — and journal entries, reports and the README have none
by construction. Quartz's local graph is dense on the same pages for a reason
that has nothing to do with the record's semantics: the generated indexes link
every document they list, so the page-link graph is dense everywhere the typed
graph is empty. Replacing would have traded a neighbourhood on every page for
an empty box on most of them. So the lineage graph is an addition, on the 58
pages that have lineage, and `Component.Graph` stays. That deviation from the
literal ask is the main thing to know about this change.

**Half the lineage was invisible until principles resolved to anchors.** The
first working version dropped any neighbour the site does not publish as a page
— a sound rule, since a node that links nowhere is worse than an absent node.
But design principles *are* published: as anchors in one assembled document,
not as a page each. Measured, **50 of 122 typed-edge endpoints on this record
are principle codes**, all of them silently dropped. The fix is not a second
resolver — `doc_refs.wikilink_target(code, scheme.output)` already answers with
the bare `#anchor` when cited from the assembled document itself, which is
exactly the string needed ([DP-4](../../record/principles.d/DP-004.md)). Pages with a graph went from 33 to 58.

**A nested record cannot spell its own URLs.** Each example under `examples/`
is staged by its own config and then mounted at `content/examples/<name>/`.
Its config has never heard of that mount point, so a URL built from the child's
own `base_url` came out as
`https://dmarx.github.io/luria/record/boundaries.d/BOUNDARY-001` — the
`examples/constitution/` prefix missing, every node a 404. Caught by looking at
the staged output rather than by a test; the parent now passes the child a
`url_base` (and the shared asset URL), and an empty string means "explicitly
none" so a parent without a `base_url` yields a child with no graphs rather
than a child confidently spelling wrong ones.

**Absolute URLs are not a style choice.** The viewer only writes an `href` it
recognises as `http(s)` — a relative path is refused outright. That is what
makes `site.base_url` a hard requirement for this feature, and it is why no
`base_url` means no graphs at all rather than graphs whose nodes do nothing.

**The first render was unreadable, and only a browser said so.** Labels were
`CODE — Title` with the real titles. At 300px in a 750px content column they
ran off the canvas and overlapped each other; the picture was worse than the
table it was supplementing. Nodes are labelled with the code alone now — the
record line two lines up states every one of these edges in prose, so the graph
carries the shape and the prose carries the words. Titles are still in each
node's `attrs`. Verified by driving the staged block in a real browser: 14,552
non-transparent canvas pixels, four nodes, three edges, no console errors, and
a click on a node issuing a request to
`https://dmarx.github.io/luria/record/decisions.d/ADR-028` (intercepted, so the
navigation is observed rather than inferred).

**Driving it also found a bug upstream.** The viewer's inspector empty state
said "Click a node to see its data" — on a page where `navigateOnClick` is set,
a click opens the node's page and the inspector never appears, so that was a
promise it could not keep. Fixed in strata-g along with the discovery that
`navigateOnClick` and `legend` had *no test coverage at all*: no export that
app produces sets either, so this was the first consumer to touch them. They
now have browser tests there, driven by editing the exported data island the
way a third-party producer does.

**The viewer is vendored with a content-hash pin**, and the behaviour the pin
protects is tested upstream, not here. A browser is not a dependency this
package will take on to re-check that a canvas draws; what it *can* check is
that the payload it ships is byte-for-byte the one those tests cover
([ADR-016](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-016.md)'s offline-drift rule, applied to a vendored asset). Verified that
the asset actually ships: built a wheel and listed
`luria/assets/strata_graph_viewer.js` inside it, because hatchling's
`packages = ["luria"]` including non-Python files is the kind of thing that is
true until it isn't.

**And then it shipped, and the built site said it was broken.** A manual
`workflow_dispatch` of the Pages workflow on the branch failed — at `deploy`,
which is a one-second environment refusal because GitHub Pages only deploys
from the default branch, and nothing to do with this change. But `build`
succeeded, which meant there was a **built-site artifact** to look at. Every
one of the 58 pages carried a data island whose quotes had been replaced with
curly ones and whose `</script>` had been moved. The feature was dead on the
real site and the local verification had said it was fine, because the local
verification put the block in a plain HTML page and skipped the markdown
pipeline entirely.

**Two causes, and only the first is the producer's fault.** CommonMark opens
an HTML block only when the tag is **alone on its line**; sharing the line
with the data island made the whole thing a paragraph of inline HTML, so the
typographer ran over it. Reproduced in seconds with `markdown-it-py` — a
different implementation of the same spec Quartz's remark follows — and fixed
with two newlines. That got rid of the curly quotes and the relocated tag.

It did **not** fix it. A clean HTML block still fails, because Quartz goes
remark → hast → **preact**, and a script element's text children are escaped
on the way out. Script content is raw text, so the browser never decodes those
entities back: `JSON.parse` throws. Verified by reading the island in a real
browser on a real build — `{&quot;nodes&quot;: […`, `parses: false`,
`mounted: false`.

**The fix came from a probe, not from reasoning.** Four carriers on one page,
built with the real Quartz and read in a real browser:

| carrier | result |
|---|---|
| `<script type="application/json">` island | **FAILS** — entity-escaped |
| JSON in a `data-graph` attribute | OK |
| base64 in the island | OK |
| base64 in an attribute | OK |

An attribute value is the one place HTML escaping round-trips by construction:
whatever a serializer escapes, the parser decodes. strata-g's viewer now reads
either carrier, and this emits the attribute. Base64 was rejected for being
opaque — a reader viewing source should see the graph, not a decode step.

**Verified the whole way this time**: `luria site` → Quartz v4.5.2 → 58 pages,
all 58 attributes parsing as JSON through an HTML parser, then one page driven
in a browser: 7 nodes / 6 edges, the legend rendered, 5,913 opaque canvas
pixels, the empty state reading "Click a node to open it.", Quartz's own
`.graph-container` still on the page, and a click on `ADR-012` issuing a
request for `record/decisions.d/ADR-012`.

**The lesson worth keeping:** a markdown generator's output is not verified
until something has parsed it as markdown. The tests now run a CommonMark
parser, and read the attribute back through an HTML parser rather than slicing
it out of the string — because the round-trip is the claim being made.

**Known limitation, stated rather than discovered later:** the graph does not
follow the site's theme toggle. The viewer paints canvas labels with literal
2D-context colours, so a `var(--light)` would be dropped by half the widget —
CSS custom properties cross a shadow boundary, but a 2D context does not read
them. It is drawn as one dark figure that reads on both Quartz themes. Fixing
it properly needs a re-theme hook in the viewer upstream.

<a name="20260912022705"></a>

## A graph you drew, on every page, instead of the one Quartz computes

*2026-09-12 02:27:05 · site · record*

**Both graphs a luria site can show are computed; neither is one anybody drew.**
Quartz's is the page-link neighbourhood, the lineage graph
([ADR-tmpronup](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-tmpronup.md)) is the typed edges — honest, automatic, and neither of them
a picture of what the project *is*. A project that knows its own shape had no
way to say so. `[luria.site] graph` is that way: point it at a strata-g
`Canvas — graph data (JSON)` export and the picture you laid out replaces
`Component.Graph` on every page.

**Replacing is right here and was wrong for lineage, for one reason: density.**
The argument against swapping Quartz's graph for the lineage graph was measured
— 47% of scheme documents have any typed edge, so most pages would have got a
box with nothing in it. A configured graph is the same picture everywhere.
There is no page it is empty on, so there is no page the swap makes worse. And
two graphs stacked above every document's first paragraph is not something
anyone chooses on purpose.

**The strata-g half was a thirty-line plugin, because the plugin kind already
existed.** `Canvas — graph data (JSON)` writes the bare `GraphExportView` that
the webapp and embed formats already inline into their HTML. Bare, with no
envelope and no version marker: the island's shape is already the contract, so
an envelope would create a second shape of the same data and hand every
consumer an unwrapping step. The `exporters` kind meant adding a format was a
file, which is exactly what that ADR was for.

**Two bugs the tests found before a build did**, which is the reversal worth
recording after the last entry. The viewer asset was written only when the
*lineage* count was non-zero, so a project with a configured graph and no typed
edges anywhere got an element and no script to mount it. And `graph` set
without a `base_url` did nothing at all, silently — the viewer is served from
the site root, which needs a site to have a root. Both are now in the staging
report rather than in the reader's empty box.

**A real export is a test fixture, not a hand-written imitation.** The contract
between the two projects is a file format, and a fixture written here to match
what this module expects would pass forever while the two drifted apart. So
`tests/fixtures/strata_g_export.json` came out of strata-g's actual export
dialog, driven through its real UI, and one test does nothing but feed it to
the loader.

**Verified against a real build, and this time that included the picture.**
`luria site` with the key set → Quartz v4.5.2 → the page carries two graphs
(the configured map and the page's lineage), `Component.Graph` is gone from the
layout, the site graph sits above the document's `# ` heading where Quartz's
was, and a click on a spoke issued a request for `docs/decisions/README`. No
page errors.

**Measured rather than guessed: the panel scrolls at the default height.** At
320px the side panel wants 198px and gets 143px, because the stacked layout
caps it at 45%. Nothing is lost — it is `overflow-y: auto` — and raising the
default would cost every page the height to save one scroll. `graph_height` is
the dial for a project that wants it taller.

**Not enabled on this record.** The capability is here and the key is
documented, but which graph luria's own site shows is a picture somebody has to
draw, and inventing one would be deciding for the project what its front door
looks like on every page.

<a name="20260912065231"></a>

## A morphing SPA and a label that was never bound

*2026-09-12 06:52:31 · site · graph*

**Two reports off the deployed site, one afternoon apart: the embedded map did
not follow you when you navigated, and every node was labelled with a bare
code.** Both were real, neither was where I would have guessed, and the second
one turned out to be sitting on a strata-g bug that makes the obvious fix
impossible.

**The map did not follow you because Quartz morphs the DOM instead of replacing
it.** Clicking a node in the graph worked — that is an ordinary full page load,
so the custom element is constructed fresh and mounts its data. Arriving at the
same page through any other link did not: Quartz's SPA router fetches the new
document and *morphs* the existing tree into it, so the `<strata-g-graph>`
element survives with a new `data-graph` attribute on it and an already-mounted
graph inside. `connectedCallback` had already fired; nothing fired again. The
element had no reason to look at its attribute a second time, so the previous
page's neighbourhood stayed on screen looking perfectly plausible.

The fix is upstream in the viewer, not here: `observedAttributes` /
`attributeChangedCallback` on `data-graph`, with `render()` tearing the previous
graph down — destroying it, dropping it from the `window.__strataGGraphs`
registry and releasing the `__strataGExport` handle — before mounting the new
one (`strata-g#786`). This record re-pins the vendored asset and its hash.

**Verified against a real build, with a positive control.** Navigating
`ADR-042 → ADR-005` by an ordinary prose link, then hard-reloading the
destination and comparing: with the newly vendored viewer both graphs on the
page match the reload exactly (26 nodes and 6, against an attribute that says 26
and 6) and the registry holds two instances. With the *previously* vendored
viewer, the same script leaves the map at **13** nodes — [ADR-042](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-042.md)'s
neighbourhood, on [ADR-005](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-005.md)'s page — while the attribute beside it says 26, and
the registry has grown to **5** leaked instances. A check that cannot fail on
the old build is not a check.

**The labels were bare codes because the recipe said so — and the fix I reached
for first does not exist.** Step 5 of `docs/graphs/README.md` bound **Label by**
to `code`, with a note claiming it was load-bearing: that merged nodes would
otherwise "inherit the vault node's long title and collide into a paragraph".
The honest correction is that titles are what makes a map navigable at all. A
code is an address; `ADR-001`, `DP-004`, `ADR-093` tells a reader nothing they
did not already have from the URL.

The obvious repair — a computed column that truncates the title with an ellipsis
so the 60-character cut is not mid-word — is accepted by the UI and silently
ignored. strata-g stamps virtual columns onto nodes *after* it stamps labels and
runs its label merge, so binding **Label by** to one falls through to `title`.
The select reads back the value you chose; the canvas never sees it. Filed as
[strata-g#787](https://github.com/dmarx/strata-g/issues/787), and the measurement
that proved it is in the export itself, which carries the computed value in
`attrs.name` and the unrelated `title` in `label`.

**The same investigation killed a claim this repository was making.** Both the
recipe and the changelog said the two layers "merge on filename". They do not.
strata-g's label merge groups by the on-screen LABEL, and the two layers title
the same document differently — the record layer prefixes the code
(`ADR-001: Four layers of record…`), the vault layer reads the bare heading. Of
the 454 nodes, 120 merge (where the two labels coincide by accident: a changelog
fragment's title *is* its timestamp) and **112 documents render as two nodes**.
A computed column stripping the `CODE: ` prefix would make the labels identical
and fold them together, which is exactly the thing `strata-g#787` blocks. The
docs now say what is true and name the bug rather than describing an
architecture the file does not have.

<a name="20260912215952"></a>

## Two halves of one fix: a page to cite, and a citation that points at it

*2026-09-12 21:59:52 · site · record*

**The first version of this change shipped the configurable half alone, and it
was right about everything except whether it helped.** `[[ADR-094]]` adds a
`cite` key choosing whether a citation resolves to a document's own page or to
an anchor in the view it assembles into. Shipped by itself, with the default
left at today's behaviour, it passed every test, rewrote nothing, and fixed
nothing — which is what the reviewer noticed within the hour: *"I ran the Pages
workflow off this branch, and the DP links still resolve to `output#anchor`."*

**Dogfooding it was the experiment that found the missing half.** Setting
`cite = "page"` in this repository's own `luria.toml` and running `luria repair`
rewrote 98 files — and staging went from **10 links redirected to the repository
to 195**. A page target points at `record/principles.d/DP-003.md`, and
`publishable()` did not publish that file: it excluded any source whose links
are spelled for somewhere else, which a design principle's are. So the site did
the only thing it could and sent every one of those readers to GitHub. That is
strictly worse than the bug being fixed — a dead anchor at least lands you on
the principles document with the content on it, at the wrong scroll position.

The lesson is narrow and worth keeping: **a link target is only better than
another if the thing it names is published.** Nothing in the record could have
told us otherwise, because `luria lint` checks that a relative target exists on
disk and `record/principles.d/DP-003.md` does. Staging is the only check that
reads a link as something a reader would try to follow, and it is a count in a
report rather than a failure.

**So the second half is publishing the sources.** `publishable()` excluded them
by a *derived* rule — `link_base(path) != path.parent`, "are this file's links
spelled for somewhere else?" — and the derivation is good. What was wrong is
that a design principle answers yes for a completely different reason than a
changelog fragment does. A fragment has no code, no title of its own, nothing to
give a page to. A principle is numbered, titled, statused, versioned and cited
by code: every property a decision has except an address. The rule now says what
it meant, and the exception is to the *consequence* rather than to the rule —
those links really are spelled for `docs/`, so `_rebase` re-points them as the
page is written, leaving the repository spelling alone because the fixer and the
lint both depend on it.

**Verified on real builds either side, because the failure mode was invisible to
everything else.** 330 broken anchor links across 81 pages → **0**; links to a
principle's page 85 → **404, all resolving**; 281 → 307 staged pages. The number
that mattered most was the boring one: links redirected to the repository went
**10 → 12**, not 195, which is how you know the new pages absorb the new targets
instead of leaking them off-site.

**Two tests changed their claim rather than their threshold, which is the right
kind of test change.** `test_publishable_is_exactly_the_files_whose_links_resolve
_in_place` asserted `link_base(path) == path.parent` over the whole corpus —
identical to the rule while no exception existed, and now a sharper statement
with the exception named. The nested-record test proved its point by the child's
document-scheme source being *absent* from the parent's staging, which this
change legitimately makes present; it now proves the same point by the presence
of the code **alias**, since only a config that knows the child's scheme can
mint one. Both were load-bearing and neither was relaxed.

**One small thing the fixer could not do.** Two links were spelled
`design-principles.md#6-fire-before-trusting` — a heading slug no rule this
project has ever emitted, so `retarget_view_citations` correctly refused to
guess at them. Rewriting them by hand would have been the third hand-written
path target in a file where hand-written paths are exactly the hazard; writing
`[[DP-6]]` and letting `luria repair` spell it is the move.
